newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore opposes U.S. plan to cut phone rates.
newsitem.headline: Singapore opposes U.S. plan to cut phone rates.

text.p: Singapore Telecommunications Ltd (SingTel) has written to the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) opposing the FCC's move to cut international phone accounting rates, the Sunday Times said.

The state-owned phone monopoly said the FCC should instead consider banning "callback" services, which let customers make international calls via another country with cheaper phone charges, the newspaper said.
Accounting rates are used to decide how much a phone company in one country pays another for completion of an international phone call.
The newspaper quoted a SingTel letter dated February 7 saying cutting accounting rates would only benefit the United States at the expense of other countries.

"SingTel strongly urges the FCC to work through the International Telecommunication Union to achieve a consensus on global acounting rate reform to the benefit of all countries, not just the United States," it quoted the letter as saying.

The FCC, the U.S. telecoms regulator, said in December it wanted to cut unilaterally the level of accounting rate payouts, which are levied when there is an imbalance in the phone traffic between two countries.
Far more calls are made from the U.S. to other countries than from other countries into the U.S., leaving U.S. carriers with an annual bill of some $5 billion, the newspaper said.
This imbalance has ballooned since the introduction of "callback" phone services.

These services, mainly operated by U.S. firms, offer, for a small fee, to call back overseas customers and provide them with a U.S. dial-tone, allowing them to pay cheaper U.S. charges for international calls.
Since 1990, the in-out ratio between U.S.-billed and Singapore-billed phone traffic on the U.S.-Singapore route had risen from 1:1 to 3:1, the newspaper quoted SingTel as saying.
On this route, SingTel estimated, more than half of all U.S.-billed traffic originated in a country other than the U.S.
